title: THE LANGUAGE THAT COULD ONLY BE OWED
deck: Ten old speakers of a river language will not let it be recorded, because Aru can be spoken only between two people who owe each other something; five weeks before the grant ends, Illuminara accepts a spoon of jam, tests her theory of the grammar against its strongest rival, and finds out what a debt needs in order to be real.
shape: Nine scenes across eight weeks: a recording that speaks only to the dead, a spoon of jam and eleven buckets of water, a young man who is paid to be a parrot, a board officer's honest arithmetic and her rival grammar, a coat sold once and lent once behind a blanket, a kitchen table with two refusals, a girl who leaves and comes back, a first frost with a price paid for it, and a word that cannot be repaid to the one who gave it.

scenes.title: The Form for Rain
paragraphs: *Harrow Landing school, recording room · the first day, 09:10*

The recording room smelled of warm dust and new foam, and Sefa Dray played the old woman's voice before Illuminara had her coat off. It was a good voice, dry and patient, eleven syllables to a breath, and it said something about a kettle. Illuminara had spent most of her working life standing between two people who shared no word, and she knew the sound of a sentence that was not being said to anybody. This was one. Every verb in it ended on the same soft closing vowel, as if the old woman were reading out the weather.

**Sefa Dray**  
Orrel Tane, five years ago. Forty hours, and it is the last clean set we have. Since then they sit with us and talk, but not into the microphone. I have ten speakers, an average age of eighty-one, and a grant that ends in six weeks.

**Illuminara**  
Why does every verb end the same way?

**Sefa Dray**  
Default ending, the linguist said. Aru has three. That is the plain one.

A hand reached past Illuminara's shoulder and pressed the pad on the machine. The kettle went silent in the middle of its boiling. A short, heavy woman in a green cardigan stood there with a jar held against her chest like an infant.

**Ilu Marwen**  
That is the ending we use for rain, and for the dead. Orrel Tane is not dead. She sat in that chair for forty hours and spoke to a box as if the box were a funeral.

**Sefa Dray**  
She agreed to it, Ilu.

**Ilu Marwen**  
She agreed to a grant. Ask her again, in Aru, and see what verb she answers with.
Sefa Dray opened her mouth, shut it, and looked at the floor, which Illuminara counted in her favour.

**Illuminara**  
You are Ilu Marwen. You have refused the board four times.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Five, counting this one. And you are the interpreter, the one who is to make the machine work, which means you will want to learn us so that we can be kept.

**Illuminara**  
I was asked to make the recording work. I would like to know what it is for before I decide whether it can.

**Ilu Marwen**  
You want to learn it so it can be kept. We want it learned so that someone can be asked for something in it. Those are not the same task, and the board has only ever paid for the first.

**Sefa Dray**  
Because the first is the only one that outlasts you. When the last of you goes, a kettle in a file is what is left.
Ilu turned to her without any heat at all.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Yes. That is a good fear. I would have it too, in your chair.
*Three endings,* Illuminara thought. *One for rain and the dead. What are the other two for?*

**Illuminara**  
Tell me what the other two are.

**Ilu Marwen**  
I will, if you ask properly.

**Illuminara**  
How do I ask properly?

Ilu unscrewed the jar, took a spoon from her cardigan pocket as if she had been carrying it for years against exactly this afternoon, and held out a heap of dark jam that smelled of smoke and berries.

scenes.title: A Spoon of Jam
paragraphs: *Ilu Marwen's kitchen, Harrow Landing · the same afternoon, 15:30*

The kitchen had one window, and the river ran past it, brown and low. By the door stood a blue enamel jar, empty to the bottom, and a bucket with a rope handle. Illuminara ate the jam and it was the best thing she had tasted on Teshun, and she said so, in the common speech, and Ilu shook her head as though a plate had been dropped.

**Ilu Marwen**  
In Aru you cannot take a thing without the verb saying who owes. You may not say it was good and leave it there. Say it again, and mean the weight.

**Illuminara**  
Then teach me the verb.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevma. I ask, and I owe the asking. It ends in the first of the two endings, the one that points at the speaker. Say it.
Illuminara said it. Her tongue had no trouble. Ilu listened with her head to one side, the way a woman listens to a pan she suspects of being cracked.

**Ilu Marwen**  
It is a word. It has no weight. You said it as if nobody was owed.

**Illuminara**  
I can learn every word the board recorded by tonight, Ilu. I can say it all perfectly. I do not think that is what you mean.

**Ilu Marwen**  
No. You could say the whole forty hours and not once be speaking. Perfect Aru with nobody in it is the rain ending in a good coat.

Illuminara put the spoon down. She had been given things all her life, power and insight and the long attention of a great many people, and she could not remember the last time she had been handed something and been unable to give it back in the same minute.

**Illuminara**  
What do I owe you?

**Ilu Marwen**  
The jar by the door is empty. The well is at the bottom of the lane, four hundred paces. Fill the jar by hand.
*By hand.* Illuminara looked at the bucket, and then, for the length of one breath, at the well she could not see, and Ilu saw her do it.

**Ilu Marwen**  
I have watched you look at pipes. Do not make the water come. I would know the difference by the taste.

So she walked the lane with a bucket. The rope bit her palm on the second trip, and by the fourth she had forgotten to be clever; the word went with her, tevma, tevma, in time with the water slopping on her boots, and somewhere around the sixth bucket it stopped being a word and became the weight in her arm. On the eleventh trip she emptied the bucket into the blue jar and the jar was full, and her shoulders ached in a plain animal way she found she was glad of.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Now ask me.

**Illuminara**  
Tevma. I ask what the other two endings are for, and I owe the asking.
Ilu closed her eyes for a moment, and then answered in a voice that had changed shape, lower and rounder, a voice that had stepped across a threshold.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevsa. You asked, and I owe you the answer. The second ending points at the other person. Ma, I owe you. Sa, you are owed. And the third is the one the board has. O. Nobody owes anybody. Rain, and the dead.
The river went on past the window. Illuminara found she was smiling like a person who has been let into a house.

**Illuminara**  
Then the grammar is a ledger.

**Ilu Marwen**  
It is a ledger that can talk. That is the only reason it has lasted ten thousand years on a river that floods.

scenes.title: Forty Cents a Word
paragraphs: *Harrow Landing school, side corridor · the third day, 18:40*

Teo Marwen was nineteen and waited at the end of the corridor with a satchel and the look of a person with an appointment he did not want. He was Ilu's great-nephew, and he had been the board's best reader for two years.

**Teo Marwen**  
You are the one Aunt Ilu fed. Everyone in the lane knows. She has not fed anyone since my grandmother died.

**Illuminara**  
I carried eleven buckets for a spoon of jam.

**Teo Marwen**  
Then you already do it better than I do. I get forty cents a word. I read the lists into the machine, six hours a day. I am very good. The linguist says I have the cleanest vowels on the river.

**Illuminara**  
And when you speak Aru to your aunt?
He did not answer for long enough that the corridor lights buzzed and clicked off on their timer. Neither of them moved to wake them.

**Teo Marwen**  
She answers me with the rain ending. Every time. I thought I was bad at it. I thought there was a part of the language that you had to be born into and I had missed it, and that I was the one who had taken the money for something I could not even do.

Illuminara could see a shape then, the way a floor plan comes clear when someone opens the last door. It did not take the languages of forty courts to see it. It took a nineteen-year-old with clean vowels and a pay slip.

**Illuminara**  
Teo. You are not bad at it. You are excellent. Here is what I think, and I can be wrong about it: the board pays you for every word, so every word you say is already settled. Nobody owes anybody, and the verb has nowhere to put the weight. Your aunt may not be rejecting your Aru. She may be answering the only grammar you have given her to answer.

**Teo Marwen**  
The money cancels it?

**Illuminara**  
If I am right, every debt, before it is made. I would not bet your aunt's kitchen on it yet.
He sat down on the floor with the satchel in his lap. It was a long time before he spoke, and when he did, it was in the common speech, very low.

**Teo Marwen**  
Bashe Corrin will not speak to me at all since I started. She is ninety-one. She taught my mother. She turned her chair to the wall when I came in last spring.

**Illuminara**  
She may not think you are bad at it. She may think you have been bought.

**Teo Marwen**  
What do I owe her, then?

**Illuminara**  
That is for her to say, and for you to ask. I only know that it cannot be money, and that it must be something she may refuse.

She did not tell him that the thing in his satchel, the forty hours of his own flawless reading, had frightened her more than the empty river had. If she was right, the unowed Aru was complete. A thousand patient hours could keep it exactly as it was, a language laid out like a body for the funeral.

scenes.title: The Arithmetic
paragraphs: *Board office, Harrow Landing · the ninth day, 10:00*

Sefa Dray had made tea in two mugs and put the sugar between them like a treaty. Her desk calendar had five weeks left on it, and the last week was marked in red by someone whose handwriting looked like her own.

**Sefa Dray**  
I will say it plainly, so that you cannot say I hid it. Hale Orne has a heart that the clinic gives four months. Bashe Corrin is ninety-one. In five weeks one of them may be a name on a stone, and if the board has not recorded what she carries, nothing of it exists. I am not afraid of kitchens. I am afraid of a grammar lesson going down a hole with her.

**Illuminara**  
You are right to be afraid of it.

**Sefa Dray**  
Then why am I being asked to bet the last ten voices on a custom about jam?
It was the strongest thing anyone had said to her on Teshun, and Illuminara let it stand a moment before she answered.

**Illuminara**  
You are not being asked to bet them. You are being asked not to spend them. The recording as it stands is fluent and dead, and a hundred hours more only makes a longer corpse. What I can offer is smaller and less safe: young people who owe old people something real, and a language that has somewhere to live.

**Sefa Dray**  
And who pays them?

**Illuminara**  
Nobody pays them. Pay the learner and the debt is cancelled. But some things must not depend on a young person's debt at all. Nursing. Winter fuel. The clinic run. Those the board pays for, to the elders directly, whether any apprentice stays or goes, so that no child is ever the only thing between an old woman and the cold. What the apprentices owe is what only a person can owe: time, errands, being there, the carrying.
Sefa looked at the calendar. She was not stupid, and she was not unkind. She was doing the arithmetic she was paid to do.

**Sefa Dray**  
Now let me be unkind, since you are being kind to me. Anselm Voy wrote the grammar, twenty years on this river. Voy never heard debt in those endings. Voy heard the room. Rain and the dead are said out of doors to the whole lane; ma and sa at a table with the door shut. Who is listening, how formal the place is. Teo's trouble is that a microphone is a room with no one in it. Pay him or do not, it changes nothing, and you have built my winter on jam.

**Illuminara**  
It is a good account. It fits everything I have heard as well as mine does.

**Sefa Dray**  
Then you do not know.

**Illuminara**  
I do not know. And you have just told me how to find out. Voy and I expect different things. If it is the room, then a formal, public, witnessed exchange will bring out ma and sa even when nothing is owed. If it is the owing, a plain private favour will, and the public, paid one will not. The paid one must be finished before a word is said: the thing handed over, the money in the hand, nothing left to return and nothing left to do. The favour must leave exactly one duty, taken freely. The same two speakers, the same new sentence, one that is not in the forty hours. Ilu and Hale Orne listen from the next room and say which ending they hear. Not me. I have told Ilu what I think; Hale has not heard it, and she speaks first.
Sefa Dray found an envelope in her drawer, wrote on a slip of paper, and sealed it with the flat of her thumb. Illuminara wrote hers on the back of a bus ticket and handed it over to be kept.

**Sefa Dray**  
If it falls Voy's way, there is no programme. I record, and you go home.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Sefa Dray**  
And if it falls yours, I still need something that can fail in public. I will not fund a feeling.

**Illuminara**  
Then name the test.

**Sefa Dray**  
By first frost, in five weeks. At least six elder and apprentice pairs, speaking Aru in the owed endings, witnessed by someone who is not you. If it is fewer, the money returns to recording and I do not apologise for it.

**Illuminara**  
That is fair. They may also refuse me entirely. I have not been accepted yet.

**Sefa Dray**  
I know. I asked Ilu this morning whether you were any good, and she said you had eleven buckets of water in you and had not spilled a drop on her floor.

scenes.title: Behind the Blanket
paragraphs: *Hale Orne's front room, Harrow Landing · the tenth day, 17:00*

Hale Orne lay on three pillows with her feet against a hot-water bottle and the face of a woman who had made her peace with dying and not with being bored. A grey blanket hung across the kitchen doorway on a length of clothesline. Ilu sat beside the bed with her knitting in her lap, not knitting. Illuminara had the floor by the door. On the sideboard lay a sealed envelope and a bus ticket, and from behind the blanket came the sounds of two people trying not to scrape their chairs.

**Hale Orne**  
Four months, the clinic says. I will give you this afternoon. Do not make me hear anything twice.

**Ilu Marwen**  
You will hear what you hear.
Sefa had tossed a coin in the yard to decide the order, and had told no one how it fell.

A bell rang in the kitchen. Someone read out terms in the flat voice of a person reading a receipt: a coat, sold outright to Teo Marwen, forty cents, paid and handed over; nothing kept back and nothing to bring back. A pen scratched. At the door a third person coughed, the school caretaker, who had been brought to stand witness and had been told to say nothing. Then Teo's voice came through the blanket, the clean vowels of the best reader on the river, saying a sentence that was in none of the forty hours.
*You put the coat in my hands.* Every verb in it closed on the same soft vowel.

**Hale Orne**  
Rain.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Rain. A man at a market.

The caretaker's boots went out and the door shut. The light under the blanket changed to a lamp's. Something was said too low to hear, and a long quiet followed, and then Teo again, with the same sentence in the same clean voice, and it was not the same sentence. The verb in its middle leaned toward the other person and stayed there. After it, a half-breath late, like a foot finding a stair that is not there, Sefa's voice answered.

**Hale Orne**  
Ma. And she gave him the sa, though she was slow with it. He is frightened he will break it.

**Ilu Marwen**  
He is frightened for the right reason.
The blanket was lifted aside. Teo came through with Sefa behind him, and Sefa took the envelope from the sideboard and opened it with a thumbnail, as if it might bite.

**Sefa Dray**  
I wrote: both of them ma and sa. The room does it. The bell, the receipt, the witness. I wrote Voy.

**Illuminara**  
Mine says the first would be rain and the second ma. I did not see the order. I only wrote what I would be wrong about.

**Hale Orne**  
You wrote the failing guess down. Nobody ever does that.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Voy was not stupid, Sefa. Listen. A debt wants somebody to hear it closed. That is why we have the lane. Voy heard the closing, and the closing wants a witness, and he took it for the owing.

**Sefa Dray**  
Then the room matters.

**Ilu Marwen**  
For the closing. Not for the owing.

**Illuminara**  
Teo. What happened in the kitchen, the second time?

**Teo Marwen**  
She held the coat out and said keep it till you are warm, and she looked at the window while I decided.

**Illuminara**  
Which meant you had to bring it back.

**Teo Marwen**  
Tomorrow, washed. I said I would, and I meant it.

**Hale Orne**  
She looked at the window. She left you the door.

**Teo Marwen**  
I could have said no.

**Hale Orne**  
There. That is what I would have told your Voy, if he had asked an old woman instead of a book. The first coat was bought and finished, and nobody owed anybody for it. The second was lent, and you took on one duty by your own say-so. Had she stood over you and said take it, you would owe her nothing at all. A thing forced is nobody's. We have the rain ending for that too. You cannot owe what you could not refuse.

**Ilu Marwen**  
That is the part I had not said aloud.
Illuminara found that she had stood up without meaning to. The design she had carried into Sefa's office had one more beam under it than she had known, and it was this one.

**Illuminara**  
Then nobody can be assigned. Not by the board, not by me, not by an elder's need. Every morning is asked again, and either of them may say no.

**Hale Orne**  
Then you will lose some.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Hale Orne**  
Good. That is how you will know the rest are real. Now go away, all of you. A girl is coming to read to me and I want to look as though I have been resting.

scenes.title: Two Refusals
paragraphs: *Harrow Landing school hall, a canteen table pulled to the middle · the twelfth day, 19:00*

There were nine chairs at the table and two of them were empty, because Hale Orne was in bed and Orrel Tane had sent word that she had said all she meant to say to the board. Bashe Corrin sat at the head in a shawl with her hands folded on the table and her chair turned a quarter away from Teo, who stood by the wall with his satchel, and she had not looked at Illuminara once. Ilu sat beside her, and Sefa Dray sat at the foot with a folder she had not opened.

Illuminara laid out the design as plainly as she could, with what Hale and Ilu had heard on the tenth day: the endings came only where each party could have said no, so no one would be assigned and every morning would be asked again. Then she waited, because what came next was not hers to hurry.

**Bashe Corrin**  
My brother owed a man in the old camp. Eleven years, for a roof. The man never said the closing word and my brother never got to say it for him. He died owing. He was owed for thirty years by a man who would not close it. A debt is also a chain, girl. You would teach children to owe us, and when we are dead who opens the door?
The room did not move. It was the real thing and everyone in it knew it. Illuminara had no clever answer and did not look for one.

**Illuminara**  
You are right. A debt with no end is a chain. Everything I have said is wrong if the one who owes cannot leave.

**Ilu Marwen**  
The closing word is the creditor's. Aru has no word for the debtor to close his own.

**Illuminara**  
Then the creditor says it first. Before the first errand, the elder says the closing word aloud, in front of a witness from the lane, and the witness keeps it. How long, what for, and the word that closes it, all spoken at the start. The learner may call the witness on any morning and ask for the closing, and it is said, and the debt is closed, whether the elder is fond of them or angry or asleep. The elder may call it too. The learner may leave in the season they choose. The elder may send them off.

**Ilu Marwen**  
A closing said before there is anything to close. That is not in the forty hours.

**Bashe Corrin**  
Then it is not a chain. A chain has no key in the debtor's pocket.

**Ilu Marwen**  
It may be bad Aru. We shall see what the lane does with it.

**Bashe Corrin**  
Written words are the board's. Aloud.

**Illuminara**  
Aloud. Never written.
Bashe Corrin considered this with her mouth very small. At last she unfolded one hand and laid it flat.

**Bashe Corrin**  
That is a better rule than the one my brother had. It is not for me. I will not owe a child and I will not be owed by one. Put my name in no kitchen.

**Illuminara**  
I will not.

**Bashe Corrin**  
If anyone wishes to learn from me, they may sit at Ilu's table and listen. They will not ask me for anything.
Ilu did not argue. She had waited sixty years for this woman to say a thing she could not argue with. Instead she turned toward the foot of the table.

**Ilu Marwen**  
And your machine, Sefa Dray. You still want it.

**Sefa Dray**  
Yes. With whatever any of you will give.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Then you ask. And whoever asks, owes.

**Sefa Dray**  
The board cannot owe a person, Ilu. It can only be accountable to the funder.

**Illuminara**  
Then it can write the debt into its own charter and read it aloud at this table. A recording given by any speaker makes the board the debtor. The archive is never sold, never used to teach anyone who has not first owed an elder, and stands only as long as the apprenticeships stay free.
Sefa looked at the folder. She picked up her pen and put it down, and did a thing Illuminara had not asked of her. She turned her chair to face the old woman.

**Sefa Dray**  
Tevma. I ask for the voices, and I owe the asking.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Badly. Again.

**Sefa Dray**  
Tevma.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Better. Tevsa. You are owed the answer, and the answer is yes, from five of us. Not from Bashe. Not from Orrel. And Hale will answer for herself.
At the door, afterward, a thin hand closed on Illuminara's sleeve. Bashe Corrin had not asked anyone to help her with her stick.

**Bashe Corrin**  
You carried Ilu's water. I counted eleven buckets from my window. Nobody does that for a tourist.

**Illuminara**  
I was not being a tourist.

**Bashe Corrin**  
I know. I will tell you one thing, and you will not owe me for it. It is the sound a river makes under ice. It has no word in the common speech. We call it the glass-talking.

**Illuminara**  
Tevma, Bashe Corrin. I owe you that.

**Bashe Corrin**  
I did not ask you to.

**Illuminara**  
No. It is mine to say.

**Bashe Corrin**  
Then hear this too, and you will not owe me for it either. That boy stood against the wall for an hour tonight with his bag on his shoulder, and nobody stands an hour who is only paid. When I am in the ground, if he asks for the glass-talking, and asks as if it weighed, you may give it to him. I will not hear him say it. I am deciding it now so that nobody has to guess at my burial.

**Illuminara**  
I will give it to him if he asks like that, and not otherwise.

**Bashe Corrin**  
Not otherwise.

scenes.title: The Fifth Afternoon
paragraphs: *Hale Orne's front room · the fifth week, a Thursday, 15:00*

Merri had been sixteen for a month when she began reading to Hale Orne in the owed endings, mornings, before school. In the third week she told Hale that mornings would not do, and Hale said afternoons or nothing, and Merri said afternoons. In the fourth, with her examinations coming, she asked the neighbour from number nine to come and say the closing word. Hale, who was fond of her and had every reason to hold on, could have said no. She said: I would rather you stayed. Merri said: I know, I am asking. The neighbour said the word that Hale had spoken into her keeping on the first day, and the debt was closed, and the lane heard it, and the nurse came on Thursday as before, because the board paid the nurse and Merri had never been the only thing between Hale and the cold.
On the fifth Thursday Illuminara came to Hale's porch with a loaf from Ilu and did not go in, because she could hear the front door open and a chair drawn up, and the screen was thin.

**Hale Orne**  
The term is closed, girl. I heard the word said. You do not owe me a Thursday.

**Merri**  
I know. Nobody does.

There was a pause, and a chair, and then Merri said something in Aru that made Illuminara put the loaf down on the step. It used the closing vowel of the rain ending, the one that said nobody owes, but it leaned on it the way the first ending leans, toward the speaker, so that the sentence meant at once that nothing was owed and that she had come, and that she wanted the old woman to know she knew the difference.
Hale Orne laughed until she coughed.

**Hale Orne**  
Seventy years, and nobody has said that to me. That is neither one thing nor the other. Ilu will call it vile grammar and then say it at supper.

**Merri**  
Is it allowed?

**Hale Orne**  
I have no idea. I have not been asked for a ruling. Read to me. Not the lists. The one with the dog.

Illuminara listened to the paper turn. Hale Orne died on the Sunday of that week, with the girl in the chair and the book open on the quilt, and the closing word was spoken at the bedside by the old woman herself in her last clear hour. It was not for the term, which had ended. It was the one she kept for what she had been given.

scenes.title: First Frost
paragraphs: *Ilu Marwen's kitchen · the sixth week, first frost, 07:20*

The window had frosted at its corners and the river was black behind it. In the lane outside there were people carrying things. Illuminara counted them as she came up the path, which she had not planned to do, and stopped at seven: a boy with a basket of split kindling, a girl with an old man's shopping, two teenagers with a handcart of stove-wood, and three more she did not know. None of them was carrying a recorder.

Teo was in the kitchen already, kneeling at the stove with the ash-pan. He had been there every dawn for four weeks. He and Ilu had spoken the terms aloud on the first morning in front of the neighbour from number nine, who had stood holding her coat and cried quite openly: fourteen weeks, the stove and the water and the lane errands, and the closing word held in her keeping. In the third week he had told Ilu he could not do the lane errands and the stove both with his lessons, and Ilu had said the stove, then, and the neighbour had come again to hear the new term said and cried again, as far as anyone could tell about everything. He had a bandage on one thumb, where the poker had caught him.

**Teo Marwen**  
Tevma, Aunt. I ask you for the morning words, and I owe you the asking, and I owe you for the day I let a machine hear me and not you.
Ilu stopped with the kettle in the air.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Say that last again.

**Teo Marwen**  
I owe you for the day I let a machine hear me and not you.

She put the kettle down. It was a sentence nobody in the room had ever heard, because in ten thousand years nobody on the river had needed to apologise to a machine. Teo had taken the owed ending, which was made for jam and water, and bent it, with fear and a little arrogance, to hold something the language had never carried. It did not break.

**Ilu Marwen**  
That is not in the forty hours.

**Teo Marwen**  
I know. I made it.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevsa. You are owed the answer. It is a good sentence. It is very bad grammar, and I will tell you why, and it will take all morning.

Illuminara stood in the doorway with the cold at her back and did not go in. It was not hers. She had said the first word in this house and it was not necessary that she be in the room for the thousandth.

A car had stopped at the gate. Sefa Dray got out of it in yesterday's clothes with the folder under her arm, and came up the path with the walk of someone who has been awake all night and decided against sitting down.

**Sefa Dray**  
I came in person, because it is not a thing to say to a machine. The panel met last night. They would approve a second year if the archive were opened to visiting scholars from January. I said no sale, no extraction, and nobody taught from it who has not first owed an elder. They said, then no equipment line. I said, then no equipment line.

**Illuminara**  
And the winter.

**Sefa Dray**  
Is in the board's charter, read aloud by me in the school hall with half the lane standing round it, and the panel cannot reach it. Nursing, fuel and the clinic run are paid to the elders directly, whether any apprentice stays or goes. I read the clause to the panel as well. Aloud. They did not like it. It is in the minutes.

**Illuminara**  
What did it cost?

**Sefa Dray**  
A year of the good microphones.

She did not sound sorry. She told the rest standing in the frost, while the kettle began again behind her: seven pairs by first frost, witnessed by the neighbour from number nine, who was not Illuminara. Five elders had given recordings, each after being asked by someone who then owed them a favour. Hale Orne had given hers in the third week, and struck a passage about a sister with her own hand. The archive was partial and unlovely, full of kettles and coughs and a child demanding to know what a particular noise meant, and every speaker had listened to their own and chosen what to withhold.

**Sefa Dray**  
The grant is over this morning. What is left is whatever you all do tomorrow without my money to do it with.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Then come in and sit down. It is going to be a long morning.

scenes.title: The Glass-Talking
paragraphs: *Bashe Corrin's porch, Harrow Landing · late autumn, 16:10*

Bashe Corrin had died on the eleventh day of the frost, between a Tuesday and a Wednesday, and the lane had said the rain ending for her. It was the only form that belonged to her now; no one could owe her, and she could owe no one. It sounded to Illuminara exactly as it had on the recording, a soft closing vowel, nothing weighing on it, but this time it was said by sixty people at once, standing in the cold, and the form that had been so wrong in a box was right and terrible in a crowd.

She had counted them without meaning to, as they stood round the grave. Of the seven pairs, Hale's had ended in the way pairs end. Five of the other six were still carrying, eleven days after the grant had stopped paying for anything but the winter coal and the nurse, and two of those five had spoken new terms aloud on the lane that week without anyone asking them to. The sixth had had its closing said in good order the week before the frost, and its learner stood at the back of the crowd with a basket, carrying nothing that was owed.
After the burial the porch was empty except for the chair, which had stayed turned a quarter toward the wall. Illuminara came to it alone.

She had been carrying it for six weeks: a word without terms. She had said tevma to a woman who had said she did not ask, and the debt had gone out into the world without a creditor to close it, and now the creditor had gone where none of the verbs could follow.
Ilu was already there, with the blue enamel jar under her arm.

**Illuminara**  
I owe Bashe Corrin a word, and she is dead, and I do not know what the grammar does with that.

**Ilu Marwen**  
It does something. It would not be the grammar if it did not.

**Illuminara**  
You have never told me the fourth ending.

**Ilu Marwen**  
There is not one. There is a way of closing, and it is old, and it is rarely needed in a village where people outlive their debts. A debt to the dead is closed when you are asked for the same thing by someone living, and you give it. And there is whatever Merri said to Hale Orne on her last Thursday. Ask me again in a year.
Illuminara sat down on the porch step, which was cold, and was glad of it.

**Illuminara**  
Nobody has asked me for the sound of a river under ice.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Not yet.

Footsteps on the gravel. Teo came up the path in his work coat with kindling dust on his sleeves, and stopped when he saw the chair. He was not her apprentice. He had never owed her a thing, and had never been owed by her, and it showed in how carefully he stood.

**Teo Marwen**  
Aunt told me about the word. The glass-talking. She said I might ask, if I wanted to. I have no right. Bashe Corrin never said a thing to me after the day I was paid.

**Illuminara**  
You do not have to ask.

**Teo Marwen**  
No. That is why I am asking.
He did not use the short form. He said it all, slowly, in the owed ending, as if he were setting down a heavy tray.

**Teo Marwen**  
Tevma. I ask you for the word Bashe Corrin gave you, and I owe you the asking, and when I have it I owe it to her.
Illuminara found that her throat did not work for the space of a few breaths. Then it did. She had meant to ask him one thing first, and she saw that he had already answered it.

**Illuminara**  
She left you a condition, Teo. She said it at her own table, with the lane listening, so that nobody would have to guess. If you asked, and asked as if it weighed, I was to give it to you. She said you stood against a wall for an hour with your bag on your shoulder. She said nobody does that who is only paid.

**Teo Marwen**  
She said that. About me.

**Illuminara**  
Tevsa. You are owed the answer. It is the glass-talking, Teo. It is the sound a river makes under ice, and it has no word in any speech but hers.

She told him how Bashe had said it, with her tongue pressed at the back of the teeth and the long soft fall at the end. He tried it and got it wrong, and tried it again, and this time his clean vowels did something Illuminara had not heard in two months of Aru: they cracked, very slightly, in the right place.
Ilu had not said a word. She stood with her hand on the back of the old woman's turned chair and looked at the river, which had not yet frozen and would not for a week.

**Ilu Marwen**  
The jar will be empty by morning.
Illuminara looked at her. Ilu's face was steady, the face of a woman who had nothing left to teach and one more thing to ask.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevma. Tomorrow at dawn, before the frost is off the lane. Two buckets, not eleven. I am old, and I do not require much. But I would like them carried by hand.

**Illuminara**  
Tevsa. Tomorrow, before the frost is off.
She walked back down the lane with the last of the light on the frozen puddles, and the glass-talking went with her, in Teo's cracked vowels, behind her on the path.

critic_line: Illuminara learns that Aru distinguishes a finished exchange from a freely accepted obligation, then helps elders, apprentices and Sefa build a speaker-controlled practice with bilateral exit, independently paid care and safeguards that survive the grant.

shared_strengths: A strong central idea, a language built on obligation, is worked out through lots of dialogue, a warm cast and a real test of two rival theories. Its weak points are some over-tidy resolution and procedural policy talk in the middle, plus a late stretch of summary. Readers who like humane ideas will stay with it.

A striking linguistic premise becomes an emotionally credible inquiry into reciprocity, consent, preservation, and grief. The dialogue carries both argument and character, rival explanations receive fair tests, and recurring concrete images—jam, buckets, coats, frost, glass-talking—give the ideas weight. Its length is substantial, but the escalating human stakes sustain attention.
shared_reservations: Sefa looked at the folder. She picked up her pen and put it down, and did a thing Illuminara had not asked of her. She turned her chair to face the old woman.

translation_sl.title: JEZIK, KI GA JE BILO MOGOČE LE DOLGOVATI
translation_sl.deck: Deset starih govorcev rečnega jezika ne dovoli njegovega snemanja, ker je aru mogoče govoriti le med dvema človekoma, ki drug drugemu nekaj dolgujeta; pet tednov pred iztekom nepovratnih sredstev Illuminara sprejme žlico marmelade, svojo teorijo slovnice preizkusi proti njenemu najmočnejšemu tekmecu in odkrije, kaj dolg potrebuje, da je resničen.
translation_sl.shape: Devet prizorov v osmih tednih: posnetek, ki govori le mrtvim, žlica marmelade in enajst veder vode, mladenič, plačan za papagaja, poštena aritmetika uradnice odbora in njena tekmovalna slovnica, plašč, enkrat prodan in enkrat posojen za odejo, kuhinjska miza z dvema zavrnitvama, dekle, ki odide in se vrne, prva slana s plačano ceno ter beseda, ki je ni mogoče vrniti tisti, ki jo je dala.

scenes.title: Oblika za dež
paragraphs: *Šola v Harrow Landingu, snemalnica · prvi dan, 09:10*

V snemalnici je dišalo po toplem prahu in novi peni, Sefa Dray pa je zavrtela glas starke, še preden je Illuminara slekla plašč. Glas je bil dober, suh in potrpežljiv, enajst zlogov na vdih, ter je govoril nekaj o kotličku. Illuminara je večino delovnega življenja stala med ljudmi, ki niso delili niti ene besede, in poznala je zvok stavka, ki ni bil izrečen nikomur. Ta je bil tak. Vsak glagol se je končal z istim mehkim končnim samoglasnikom, kot bi starka brala vremensko napoved.

**Sefa Dray**  
Orrel Tane, pred petimi leti. Štirideset ur, zadnji čist komplet, ki ga imamo. Od takrat sedijo z nami in govorijo, vendar ne v mikrofon. Imam deset govorcev, povprečno starih enainosemdeset let, in sredstva, ki potečejo čez šest tednov.

**Illuminara**  
Zakaj se vsak glagol konča enako?

**Sefa Dray**  
Privzeta končnica, je rekel jezikoslovec. Aru ima tri. To je navadna.
Roka je segla mimo Illuminarine rame in pritisnila ploščico na napravi. Kotliček je utihnil sredi vretja. Tam je stala nizka, čokata ženska v zeleni jopi in ob prsih držala kozarec kot dojenčka.

**Ilu Marwen**  
To je končnica, ki jo uporabljamo za dež in za mrtve. Orrel Tane ni mrtva. Štirideset ur je sedela na tistem stolu in govorila škatli, kot da je škatla pogreb.

**Sefa Dray**  
Strinjala se je, Ilu.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Strinjala se je z nepovratnimi sredstvi. Vprašajte jo še enkrat, v aru, in poglejte, s katerim glagolom bo odgovorila.
Sefa Dray je odprla usta, jih zaprla in pogledala v tla; Illuminara ji je to štela v prid.

**Illuminara**  
Vi ste Ilu Marwen. Odbor ste zavrnili štirikrat.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Petkrat, če štejem tudi to. Vi pa ste tolmačka, tista, ki naj bi usposobila napravo, kar pomeni, da se nas boste hoteli naučiti, da nas bo mogoče ohraniti.

**Illuminara**  
Prosili so me, naj snemanje usposobim. Preden se odločim, ali je to mogoče, bi rada vedela, čemu služi.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Naučiti se ga hočete, da bi ga bilo mogoče ohraniti. Mi hočemo, da se ga kdo nauči zato, da lahko v njem nekoga za nekaj prosi. To ni ista naloga, odbor pa je vedno plačeval le prvo.

**Sefa Dray**  
Ker je prva edina, ki vas preživi. Ko odide zadnji med vami, ostane kotliček v datoteki.
Ilu se je obrnila k njej brez kančka jeze.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Da. To je dober strah. Tudi mene bi bilo strah, če bi sedela na vašem stolu.
*Tri končnice,* je pomislila Illuminara. *Ena za dež in mrtve. Čemu služita drugi dve?*

**Illuminara**  
Povejte mi, čemu služita drugi dve.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Bom, če boste pravilno vprašali.

**Illuminara**  
Kako pravilno vprašam?
Ilu je odvila kozarec, iz žepa jopice vzela žlico, kot da jo že leta nosi prav za to popoldne, ter ponudila kupček temne marmelade, ki je dišala po dimu in jagodičevju.

scenes.title: Žlica marmelade
paragraphs: *Kuhinja Ilu Marwen, Harrow Landing · isto popoldne, 15:30*

Kuhinja je imela eno okno, mimo njega pa je tekla rjava in nizka reka. Ob vratih je stal moder emajliran vrč, prazen do dna, in vedro z ročajem iz vrvi. Illuminara je pojedla marmelado; bila je najboljša stvar, ki jo je okusila na Teshunu. To je povedala v skupnem jeziku, Ilu pa je odkimala, kot bi kdo razbil krožnik.

**Ilu Marwen**  
V aru stvari ne morete vzeti, ne da bi glagol povedal, kdo dolguje. Ne morete reči, da je bilo dobro, in pri tem ostati. Povejte še enkrat in mislite težo.

**Illuminara**  
Potem me naučite glagola.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevma. Prosim in dolgujem prošnjo. Konča se s prvo od obeh končnic, tisto, ki kaže na govorca. Izgovorite jo.
Illuminara jo je izgovorila. Jezik ji ni delal težav. Ilu je poslušala z glavo, nagnjeno vstran, kakor ženska posluša ponev, za katero sumi, da je počena.

**Ilu Marwen**  
To je beseda. Nima teže. Izgovorili ste jo, kot da nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje.

**Illuminara**  
Do večera se lahko naučim vsake besede, ki jo je odbor posnel, Ilu. Vse lahko izgovorim brezhibno. Mislim, da ne govorite o tem.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Ne. Lahko bi izgovorili vseh štirideset ur, ne da bi enkrat samkrat govorili. Popoln aru brez kogar koli v njem je dežna končnica v dobrem plašču.

Illuminara je odložila žlico. Vse življenje je prejemala darove, moč in vpogled ter dolgotrajno pozornost mnogih ljudi, pa se ni mogla spomniti, kdaj ji je nazadnje kdo nekaj podal, česar ni mogla vrniti v isti minuti.

**Illuminara**  
Kaj vam dolgujem?

**Ilu Marwen**  
Vrč pri vratih je prazen. Vodnjak je na dnu ulice, štiristo korakov daleč. Napolnite ga ročno.
*Ročno.* Illuminara je pogledala vedro, nato pa za en vdih vodnjak, ki ga ni mogla videti, in Ilu je to opazila.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Videla sem vas gledati cevi. Ne prikličite vode. Po okusu bi poznala razliko.

Zato je hodila po ulici z vedrom. Vrv se ji je ob drugem obhodu zarezala v dlan, do četrtega pa je pozabila biti pametna; beseda je hodila z njo, tevma, tevma, v ritmu vode, ki ji je pljuskala po škornjih, in nekje okoli šestega vedra je nehala biti beseda ter postala teža v njeni roki. Ob enajstem obhodu je vedro izlila v modri vrč; vrč je bil poln, ramena pa so jo bolela na preprost, živalski način, ki se ga je razveselila.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Zdaj me vprašajte.

**Illuminara**  
Tevma. Prosim, da mi poveste, čemu služita drugi dve končnici, in dolgujem prošnjo.
Ilu je za trenutek zaprla oči, nato odgovorila z glasom, ki je spremenil obliko, postal globlji in bolj zaobljen, glasom, ki je prestopil prag.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Tevsa. Vprašali ste in dolgujem vam odgovor. Druga končnica kaže na drugega človeka. Ma, dolgujem vam. Sa, vam se dolguje. Tretjo pa ima odbor. O. Nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje. Dež in mrtvi.
Reka je tekla naprej mimo okna. Illuminara je ugotovila, da se smehlja kot človek, ki so ga spustili v hišo.

**Illuminara**  
Potem je slovnica knjiga dolgov.

**Ilu Marwen**  
Knjiga dolgov, ki lahko govori. To je edini razlog, da je deset tisoč let preživela ob reki, ki poplavlja.

scenes.title: Štirideset centov na besedo
paragraphs: *Šola v Harrow Landingu, stranski hodnik · tretji dan, 18:40*
Teo Marwen je imel devetnajst let in čakal na koncu hodnika s torbo ter izrazom človeka, ki ima sestanek, na katerega noče. Bil je Ilujin pranečak in dve leti najboljši bralec odbora.

**Teo Marwen**  
Vi ste tista, ki jo je teta Ilu nahranila. Vsi v ulici vedo. Odkar je umrla moja babica, ni nahranila nikogar.

**Illuminara**  
Za žlico marmelade sem nesla enajst veder.

**Teo Marwen**  
Potem to že počnete bolje od mene. Dobim štirideset centov na besedo. Sezname berem v napravo šest ur na dan. Zelo dober sem. Jezikoslovec pravi, da imam najčistejše samoglasnike ob reki.

**Illuminara**  
In ko govorite aru svoji teti?
Tako dolgo ni odgovoril, da so luči na hodniku zabrnele in se po časovniku ugasnile. Nobeden od njiju se ni premaknil, da bi jih prebudil.

**Teo Marwen**  
Vedno mi odgovori z dežno končnico. Vsakič. Mislil sem, da mi ne gre. Mislil sem, da obstaja del jezika, v katerega se moraš roditi, pa sem ga zamudil, in da sem vzel denar za nekaj, česar niti ne zmorem.

Illuminara je tedaj zagledala obliko, kakor se tloris razjasni, ko nekdo odpre zadnja vrata. Za to niso bili potrebni jeziki štiridesetih dvorov. Potreben je bil devetnajstletnik s čistimi samoglasniki in plačilno listo.

**Illuminara**  
Teo. Ne gre vam slabo. Odlični ste. Mislim naslednje in lahko se motim: odbor vam plača vsako besedo, zato je vsaka izgovorjena beseda že poravnana. Nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje in glagol nima kam položiti teže. Vaša teta morda ne zavrača vašega aru. Morda odgovarja edini slovnici, ki ste ji jo dali.

**Teo Marwen**  
Denar ga izniči?

**Illuminara**  
Če imam prav, izniči vsak dolg, še preden nastane. Na to še ne bi stavila kuhinje vaše tete.
Sedel je na tla s torbo v naročju. Dolgo je trajalo, preden je spregovoril; ko je, je govoril v skupnem jeziku in zelo tiho.

**Teo Marwen**  
Bashe Corrin se, odkar sem začel, z menoj sploh ne pogovarja. Enaindevetdeset let ima. Učila je mojo mamo. Ko sem prišel lani spomladi, je obrnila stol proti steni.

**Illuminara**  
Morda ne misli, da vam ne gre. Morda misli, da so vas kupili.

**Teo Marwen**  
Kaj ji potem dolgujem?

**Illuminara**  
To mora povedati ona, vi pa morate vprašati. Vem le, da ne sme biti denar in da mora biti nekaj, kar lahko zavrne.

Ni mu povedala, da jo je stvar v njegovi torbi, štirideset ur njegovega brezhibnega branja, prestrašila bolj kakor prazna reka. Če je imela prav, je bil aru brez dolga popoln. Tisoč potrpežljivih ur bi ga lahko ohranilo natanko takega, kakršen je bil: jezik, položen kot telo za pogreb.

scenes.title: Aritmetika
paragraphs: *Pisarna odbora, Harrow Landing · deveti dan, 10:00*

Sefa Dray je skuhala čaj v dveh skodelicah in mednju položila sladkor kot mirovno pogodbo. Na njenem namiznem koledarju je ostalo pet tednov, zadnjega pa je z rdečo označil nekdo s pisavo, podobno njeni.

**Sefa Dray**  
Povedala bom naravnost, da ne boste mogli reči, da sem skrivala. Hale Orne ima srce, ki mu klinika daje štiri mesece. Bashe Corrin ima enaindevetdeset let. Čez pet tednov bo morda ena od njiju ime na kamnu; če odbor ne posname tega, kar nosi, ne bo obstajalo nič od tega. Ne bojim se kuhinj. Bojim se, da bo slovnična lekcija z njo vred padla v luknjo.

**Illuminara**  
Prav je, da se tega bojite.

**Sefa Dray**  
Zakaj se potem od mene zahteva, naj zadnjih deset glasov zastavim na običaj z marmelado?
To je bila najmočnejša stvar, ki ji jo je kdo rekel na Teshunu, in Illuminara jo je pustila trenutek stati, preden je odgovorila.

**Illuminara**  
Ne zahtevajo, da jih zastavite. Zahtevajo, da jih ne porabite. Posnetek, kakršen je, je tekoč in mrtev; sto dodatnih ur naredi le daljše truplo. Ponudim lahko nekaj manjšega in manj varnega: mlade ljudi, ki starejšim dolgujejo nekaj resničnega, ter jezik, ki ima kje živeti.

**Sefa Dray**  
In kdo jih plača?

**Illuminara**  
Nihče. Plačajte učencu in dolg je izničen. Toda nekatere stvari sploh ne smejo biti odvisne od dolga mladega človeka. Nega. Gorivo za zimo. Prevoz na kliniko. Te odbor plačuje neposredno starejšim, ne glede na to, ali kateri vajenec ostane ali odide, da otrok nikoli ne bo edino med starko in mrazom. Vajenci dolgujejo tisto, kar lahko dolguje le človek: čas, opravke, navzočnost, prenašanje.
Sefa je pogledala koledar. Ni bila neumna in ni bila neprijazna. Delala je račun, za katerega je bila plačana.

**Sefa Dray**  
Zdaj naj bom neprijazna, saj ste vi prijazni do mene. Anselm Voy je napisal slovnico; dvajset let je preživel ob tej reki. Voy v teh končnicah ni slišal dolga. Slišal je prostor. Dež in mrtvi se omenjajo zunaj, vsej ulici; ma in sa za mizo pri zaprtih vratih. Pomembno je, kdo posluša in kako uraden je kraj. Teova težava je, da je mikrofon soba brez človeka. Plačate ga ali ne, ničesar ne spremeni, vi pa ste mojo zimo postavili na marmelado.

**Illuminara**  
To je dobra razlaga. Vsemu, kar sem slišala, ustreza enako dobro kot moja.

**Sefa Dray**  
Potem ne veste.

**Illuminara**  
Ne vem. Pravkar pa ste mi povedali, kako lahko ugotovim. Voy in jaz pričakujeva različne stvari. Če odloča prostor, bo ma in sa sprožila formalna, javna, izpričana izmenjava, tudi če ni nič dolgovano. Če odloča dolg, bo to storila navadna zasebna usluga, javno plačana pa ne. Plačana mora biti zaključena, preden je izrečena beseda: stvar predana, denar v roki, ničesar več za vrniti in ničesar več storiti. Usluga mora pustiti natanko eno svobodno sprejeto dolžnost. Ista govorca, isti novi stavek, ki ga ni med štiridesetimi urami. Ilu in Hale Orne poslušata iz sosednje sobe ter povesta, katero končnico slišita. Ne jaz. Ilu sem povedala, kaj mislim; Hale tega ni slišala in govori prva.
Sefa Dray je v predalu našla ovojnico, nekaj napisala na listek in ga z ravnim delom palca zapečatila. Illuminara je svoje napisala na hrbtno stran avtobusne vozovnice ter ji jo izročila v hrambo.

**Sefa Dray**  
Če se izkaže, da ima Voy prav, programa ne bo. Jaz snemam, vi pa greste domov.

**Illuminara**  
Da.

**Sefa Dray**  
Če imate prav vi, še vedno potrebujem nekaj, kar lahko javno spodleti. Ne bom financirala občutka.

**Illuminara**  
Potem določite preizkus.

**Sefa Dray**  
Do prve slane, čez pet tednov. Najmanj šest parov starejšega in vajenca, ki govorijo aru v končnicah dolga, priča pa je nekdo, ki niste vi. Če jih bo manj, se denar vrne snemanju in za to se ne bom opravičila.

**Illuminara**  
Pošteno. Lahko me tudi v celoti zavrnejo. Nisem še sprejeta.

**Sefa Dray**  
Vem. Ilu sem danes zjutraj vprašala, ali ste kaj dobri, in rekla je, da imate v sebi enajst veder vode ter niste niti kaplje polili po njenih tleh.

scenes.title: Za odejo
paragraphs: *Sprednja soba Hale Orne, Harrow Landing · deseti dan, 17:00*

Hale Orne je ležala na treh blazinah, stopala je imela ob termoforju, obraz pa kot ženska, ki se je sprijaznila s smrtjo, ne pa tudi z dolgočasjem. Siva odeja je na vrvi za perilo visela čez kuhinjska vrata. Ilu je sedela ob postelji s pletenjem v naročju, vendar ni pletla. Illuminara je sedela na tleh pri vratih. Na omarici sta ležali zapečatena ovojnica in avtobusna vozovnica, izza odeje pa se je slišalo, kako dva človeka skušata ne podrsavati s stoli.

**Hale Orne**
